notes:
I've put together notes on Psalm 140, verse by verse, but there are real gaps. I ran out of searches before I could find any Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity-teaching material on this psalm, so those views are missing. I also didn't find traditions truly disagreeing. On vv. 9–11 they differ more in emphasis than in substance. One sorting note: Guzik (enduringword.com) is from your Pentecostal/charismatic list, but most of what he gives is quotes from older writers like Spurgeon, Kidner and Horne.

**Whole psalm (background)**
- **Author.** Guzik reads it as David being slandered, maybe while running from Saul's court (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/). Ellicott lists other suggested settings: Manasseh's reign, just after the exile, and the Maccabean era. He thinks it reads best as Israel speaking together, or one person speaking for the faithful part of the nation (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html). The Expositor's Bible says it feels to him like a later poet writing "in the Davidic manner" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/140.htm). Coffman, quoting Barnes, says there is no doubt David wrote it (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-140.html).
- **Wording.** Utley says the psalm has many rare words, and the scribes suggested corrections in vv. 10, 11 and 13, which shows the text is confused there (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-140).

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: "evil man" is singular, but this isn't a grudge against one person, because the psalm moves straight to the plural (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html). The Pulpit Commentary agrees and notes the Hebrew is literally "man of violences" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Guzik: the psalm opens with no praise first. David goes straight to his plea, which shows how urgent it is (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).
- Spurgeon: the line sounds like the Lord's Prayer's "deliver us from evil." David is praying against a type of person, not just one man (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/140-1.htm).
- Gill names Saul or Doeg, and applies the verse to the enemies of Christ and of his people (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/140-1.html).

**v. 2**
- Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary: "stir up wars" is a better reading than "gathered together." Ellicott says Israel wanted peace, but people inside and outside kept dragging her into trouble (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html).
- Utley, citing a NET Bible note: the "wars" here are probably quarrels between people, not wars between nations (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-140).
- Spurgeon calls it a "heart-disease" when someone enjoys imagining harm to others (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: their words wound as painfully as a poisoned bite. The "Selah" marks the end of the first section (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Utley: many of the Hebrew words use the "sh" sound, imitating a snake's hiss (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-140).
- Spurgeon: saying snakes poison with their tongues is poetic language, not bad science (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).
- Paul quotes this verse in Romans 3:13. Guzik says Paul widens it from David's enemies to all fallen people (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: this repeats v. 1 with changes, and the repetition shows how desperate the psalmist is. "Overthrow my goings" means to destroy him (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm). Ellicott gives the literal sense as "thrust aside my steps" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html).
- Matthew Henry: they wanted to pull him into sin and trouble, ruin his reputation, and kill him (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_140.cfm).

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: "snare… and cords" means a snare made of cords, hidden in grass or bushes like a hunter's trap (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Seedbed (Wesleyan) points out how planned the attacks are: they devise, plot, hide and spread their traps (https://seedbed.com/the-end-of-evil-psalm-140/).
- Spurgeon's preaching notes treat the "net by the wayside" as hidden temptations in daily life (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps140.cfm).

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the wording is typical of David (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Spurgeon: "You are my God" sets the Lord against the gods other nations worshipped (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).
- Calvin (Reformed): this shows real prayer coming from faith, not just words. He adds that no one prays sincerely until they are convinced God's grace saves them (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/140.htm).

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: "GOD the Lord" is Jehovah Adonai, an uncommon way to address God. God has guarded David's head in past fights, so he trusts him for the future (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: literally "day of arms," meaning the day he put on armour. Ellicott links it to the "helmet of salvation" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_140.cfm).
- Spurgeon: God had been David's armour-bearer (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: what the wicked want harms them and others, so God is being merciful when he refuses it (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Matthew Henry: the request is that their success won't make them proud, as if it proved God was on their side (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/140-9.html).
- Ellicott: the Hebrew here is damaged. The Greek and Latin versions read "give me not over… desert me not," and Paul may have had that in mind in Romans 1:24 (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html).

**v. 9**
- Pulpit and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the enemies' "head" is set against David's head in v. 7. God covers his head, but theirs is covered only by the shame of their own words (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Guzik: the "head" may be Saul or Doeg. If it's Saul, David leaves the punishment to God instead of attacking Saul himself (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).
- Coffman: this is the law of like-for-like punishment. The poison on their lips should drown them (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-140.html).

**v. 10 (the curse prayer; this is where views differ most)**
- **Wording.** The Expositor's Bible says most modern scholars change the verb to match Psalm 11:6, giving "Let Him rain coals on them" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/140.htm). Ellicott notes the Hebrew word for "pits" appears only here and may mean whirlpools or ditches (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html).
- **A prediction, not a wish.** The Pulpit Commentary says the lines declare what will happen rather than wish it (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm). Trapp says the same (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-140.cfm), and Matthew Henry says the verse can be read as a prophecy (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/140-9.html).
- **Reformed.** Calvin sees a reference to Sodom and Gomorrah's fate, which Jude presents as a lasting warning of God's judgment on the ungodly (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/140-9.html).
- **Baptist.** Spurgeon also sees Sodom here (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/). Desiring God says these curse prayers teach Christians to leave personal wrongs for God to repay. God's anger, used up either at the cross or in hell, frees believers to love their enemies (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/oh-slay-the-wicked).
- **Wesleyan.** Seedbed sets the verse beside Jesus' command to love enemies. Read through the cross, the burning coals fall on Jesus, and the prayer becomes a request that God change the wicked (https://seedbed.com/the-end-of-evil-psalm-140/).
- **Guzik.** Christians are told not to return evil for evil, yet we can feel with David's cry for justice (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/). Kidner, quoted there, takes the coals and pits as images: the coals for their burning words, the pits for the traps they set.
- **Coffman** says "the fire" is plainly hell (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-140.html). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown just call the images pictures of total destruction (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_140.cfm).
- A Bible Hub Q&A says Augustine and the early church read these curses spiritually, as a wish for sin's defeat and for evildoers to repent (https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_psalm_140_10_show_mercy.htm). I couldn't find Augustine's own text.

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: literally "a man of tongue," meaning someone who talks big but achieves nothing and won't last. "To overthrow" is plural in Hebrew, for complete ruin (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Ellicott thinks one particular loud, violent speaker may be meant (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html).
- Expositor's Bible: the hunters of v. 5 become the hunted (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/140.htm).
- Trapp notes the Aramaic paraphrase says the angel of death will hunt the violent man into hell (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-140.cfm).
- Spurgeon's notes: the man is lost forever unless he repents, but there is "another Huntsman," the Son of Man who seeks the lost (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps140.cfm).

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: the righteous will be rescued in the end. The right isn't always on the side of the poor, but when it is, God will be their champion (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Guzik, citing VanGemeren: "I know" is a victory cry (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).
- Utley suggests the psalm may come from a court case, like Psalm 139 (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-140).

**v. 13**
- Utley: "dwell in Your presence" could mean worship in the temple or life with God after death, and only context can decide (https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-140).
- Pulpit: the righteous give thanks and come to his house often (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/140.htm).
- Spurgeon's notes: "sit" before God as friends or guests, or perhaps sit enthroned (compare Matthew 19:28) (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps140.cfm).
- Ellicott: "Surely" may mean "only." Those the heathen tried to drive out end up living safely in the land (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-140.html).
- Guzik: living in God's presence is "the best reward of all" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-140/).
